impacts.conditions: The CNA description states: When used to deliver a signal to a specific thread, thr_kill2(2) called p_cansignal() to determine whether the operation was permitted but did not check the result before delivering the signal. The signal was sent even when the permission check failed. The system call returned the resulting error to the caller, but by then the signal had already been delivered. The missing check allows an unprivileged local user who knows or can guess a target's process and thread IDs to send any signal to a process they would not normally be permitted to signal, including processes owned by other users or by root. The same check enforces jail boundaries, so a jailed process can signal processes on the host or in other jails. Thread IDs are allocated globally and sequentially, and so can be discovered by brute force with no visibility into the target. An attacker can stop or terminate arbitrary processes, including critical system daemons, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS).
impacts.exploitation: Exploitation in the wild is not established by the cited description.

title: OpenSSL hexadecimal conversion heap buffer overflow
summary: OpenSSL says oversized OCTET STRING to hex conversion can overflow the heap buffer on 32-bit platforms; large untrusted certificates processed by logging/printing applications are the relevant condition. OpenSSL rates it Low and credits Quoc Tran of Xint.io.

impacts.conditions: The CNA description states: Issue summary: Converting an excessively large OCTET STRING value to a hexadecimal string leads to a heap buffer overflow on 32 bit platforms. Impact summary: A heap buffer overflow may lead to a crash or possibly an attacker controlled code execution or other undefined behavior. If an attacker can supply a crafted X.509 certificate with an excessively large OCTET STRING value in extensions such as the Subject Key Identifier (SKID) or Authority Key Identifier (AKID) which are being converted to hex, the size of the buffer needed for the result is calculated as multiplication of the input length by 3. On 32 bit platforms, this multiplication may overflow resulting in the allocation of a smaller buffer and a heap buffer overflow. Applications and services that print or log contents of untrusted X.509 certificates are vulnerable to this issue. As the certificates would have to have sizes of over 1 Gigabyte, printing or logging such certificates is a fairly unlikely operation and only 32 bit platforms are affected, this issue was assigned Low severity. The FIPS modules in 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, 3.3 and 3.0 are not affected by this issue, as the affected code is outside the OpenSSL FIPS module boundary.

title: XBOW autonomously discovers Linux SMC-D out-of-bounds write
product: Linux kernel SMC-D DIBS loopback transport
ai_system: XBOW autonomous vulnerability research agents; model not publicly identified
summary: The SMC-D loopback path failed to bounds-check a peer-controlled memory offset before copying data, creating an out-of-bounds write. XBOW says its system handled threat modeling, code auditing, discovery and validation, with humans steering several research decisions and exploit development.
ai_role: XBOW’s first-party case report says it discovered and validated this CVE and autonomously handled threat modeling, code auditing, vulnerability discovery and validation. It explicitly describes three human interventions steering the threat model and exploit strategy, so this is AI-assisted discovery, not autonomous end-to-end work.
classification_note: XBOW reports it disclosed the issue to maintainers before CVE publication; no in-the-wild exploitation is stated.
remediation_note: XBOW’s advisory lists Linux stable fixes; the kernel CVE notice is linked as vendor advisory. Check distribution-specific patch status before assuming a system is fixed.

scenarios:
AV:L - The flaw is only reachable via loopback-ISM (intra-OS DIBS), which requires matching local GID and shared kernel; exploitation is through AF_SMC sendmsg after SMC-D handshake, not remote packet handling on a network-facing stack path.
AC:L - A malicious SMC-D peer can supply crafted CLC dmbe_idx/dmbe_size values and send patterns that drive move_data() with attacker-controlled offset and size; no race or uncontrollable memory layout is required once loopback-ISM is active.
PR:L - Exploitation requires only an unprivileged local account able to open AF_SMC sockets and complete an SMC-D loopback handshake (no CAP_NET_ADMIN or root); the SMC CLC path performs no authentication beyond standard socket access controls.
UI:N - No victim user action is needed when a malicious peer initiates an inbound SMC-D connection to a listening service; the attacker can trigger the OOB write by sending SMC-D data after handshake completion.
S:U - The OOB write corrupts kernel heap memory within the same kernel security authority; successful exploitation yields local privilege escalation, not cross-VM, container-boundary, or IOMMU bypass scope change.
C:H - An out-of-bounds kernel heap write past the folio-allocated DMB buffer can corrupt adjacent kernel objects and be leveraged for arbitrary kernel memory disclosure, not merely a bounded leak or pure crash.
I:H - The unchecked memcpy() allows controlled out-of-bounds writes beyond the registered DMB allocation, enabling heap corruption and potential arbitrary kernel code execution or control-flow hijacking.
A:H - Writing past the allocated DMB folio can immediately corrupt critical kernel structures and cause kernel oops, panic, or hang; heap corruption from the OOB write itself constitutes high availability impact.

impacts.conditions: A peer-supplied out-of-bounds offset/size causes an out-of-bounds write past the allocated kernel buffer in the software SMC-D loopback path. No further consequence is stated.
impacts.exploitation: Exploitation in the wild is not established by the cited description.

impacts.conditions: When an FTP wildcard `LIST` operation fails, libcurl omits the restoration path meant for successful listings, leaving the write callback set to the internal listing parser and the write callback data pointing directly to the easy handle. CWE-416 Use After Free

title: Improper validation of PBMAC1 parameters in PKCS#12 MAC verification
ai_system: AISLE autonomous analyzer (specific model/version not disclosed)
summary: A malformed PKCS#12 file using PBMAC1 can supply unchecked PBKDF2 key length and salt parameters, causing a stack buffer overflow or invalid/NULL pointer dereference during MAC verification. OpenSSL says processing untrusted PKCS#12 files is uncommon.
ai_role: AISLE’s January 26, 2026 article says its autonomous analyzer found all 12 CVEs in OpenSSL’s January coordinated release, and individually names this case. OpenSSL’s own vulnerability record credits the named Aisle Research finder(s) for CVE-2025-11187; OpenSSL’s January 27 security advisory gives the flaw and report chronology. The exact model and division of AI versus researcher analysis are not public. Stanislav Fort and Petr Šimeček of Aisle Research are named as finders; Hamza (Metadust) independently reported the issue. The report states the AI analyzer found all 12 cases; precise AI/human contributions per defect are not described.
classification_note: OpenSSL published the vendor advisory and released fixes on January 27, 2026. The AISLE public AI attribution article appeared January 26, one day before the public vendor disclosure. No claim of in-the-wild exploitation is made.
remediation_note: OpenSSL 3.6.1, 3.5.5, 3.4.4. See the OpenSSL advisory for affected release details; FIPS impact and exceptional configurations are stated in the advisory where applicable. This record does not establish deployment.

impacts.conditions:
CNA description: Issue summary: PBMAC1 parameters in PKCS#12 files are missing validation
which can trigger a stack-based buffer overflow, invalid pointer or NULL
pointer dereference during MAC verification.

Impact summary: The stack buffer overflow or NULL pointer dereference may
cause a crash leading to Denial of Service for an application that parses
untrusted PKCS#12 files. The buffer overflow may also potentially enable
code execution depending on platform mitigations.

When verifying a PKCS#12 file that uses PBMAC1 for the MAC, the PBKDF2
salt and keylength parameters from the file are used without validation.
If the value of keylength exceeds the size of the fixed stack buffer used
for the derived key (64 bytes), the key derivation will overflow the buffer.
The overflow length is attacker-controlled. Also, if the salt parameter is
not an OCTET STRING type this can lead to invalid or NULL pointer
dereference.

Exploiting this issue requires a user or application to process
a maliciously crafted PKCS#12 file. It is uncommon to accept untrusted
PKCS#12 files in applications as they are usually used to store private
keys which are trusted by definition. For this reason the issue was assessed
as Moderate severity.

The FIPS modules in 3.6, 3.5 and 3.4 are not affected by this issue, as
PKCS#12 processing is outside the OpenSSL FIPS module boundary.

OpenSSL 3.6, 3.5 and 3.4 are vulnerable to this issue.

OpenSSL 3.3, 3.0, 1.1.1 and 1.0.2 are not affected by this issue as they do
not support PBMAC1 in PKCS#12.
impacts.exploitation: Exploitation in the wild is not established by the cited description.

title: Stack buffer overflow in CMS AuthEnvelopedData parsing
ai_system: AISLE autonomous analyzer (specific model/version not disclosed)
summary: A crafted oversized AEAD IV in CMS AuthEnvelopedData or EnvelopedData can be copied into a fixed-size stack buffer before authentication. OpenSSL says impact may be denial of service or potentially remote code execution, depending on platform/toolchain mitigations.

remediation_note: OpenSSL 3.6.1, 3.5.5, 3.4.4, 3.3.6 and 3.0.19. See the OpenSSL advisory for affected release details; FIPS impact and exceptional configurations are stated in the advisory where applicable. This record does not establish deployment.

impacts.conditions: The CNA description states: Issue summary: Parsing CMS AuthEnvelopedData or EnvelopedData message with maliciously crafted AEAD parameters can trigger a stack buffer overflow. Impact summary: A stack buffer overflow may lead to a crash, causing Denial of Service, or potentially remote code execution. When parsing CMS (Auth)EnvelopedData structures that use AEAD ciphers such as AES-GCM, the IV (Initialization Vector) encoded in the ASN.1 parameters is copied into a fixed-size stack buffer without verifying that its length fits the destination. An attacker can supply a crafted CMS message with an oversized IV, causing a stack-based out-of-bounds write before any authentication or tag verification occurs. Applications and services that parse untrusted CMS or PKCS#7 content using AEAD ciphers (e.g., S/MIME (Auth)EnvelopedData with AES-GCM) are vulnerable. Because the overflow occurs prior to authentication, no valid key material is required to trigger it. While exploitability to remote code execution depends on platform and toolchain mitigations, the stack-based write primitive represents a severe risk. The FIPS modules in 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, 3.3 and 3.0 are not affected by this issue, as the CMS implementation is outside the OpenSSL FIPS module boundary. OpenSSL 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, 3.3 and 3.0 are vulnerable to this issue. OpenSSL 1.1.1 and 1.0.2 are not affected by this issue.
impacts.exploitation: Exploitation in the wild is not established by the cited description.

impacts.conditions: The CNA description states: Issue summary: A TLS 1.3 connection using certificate compression can be forced to allocate a large buffer before decompression without checking against the configured certificate size limit. Impact summary: An attacker can cause per-connection memory allocations of up to approximately 22 MiB and extra CPU work, potentially leading to service degradation or resource exhaustion (Denial of Service). In affected configurations, the peer-supplied uncompressed certificate length from a CompressedCertificate message is used to grow a heap buffer prior to decompression. This length is not bounded by the max_cert_list setting, which otherwise constrains certificate message sizes. An attacker can exploit this to cause large per-connection allocations followed by handshake failure. No memory corruption or information disclosure occurs. This issue only affects builds where TLS 1.3 certificate compression is compiled in (i.e., not OPENSSL_NO_COMP_ALG) and at least one compression algorithm (brotli, zlib, or zstd) is available, and where the compression extension is negotiated. Both clients receiving a server CompressedCertificate and servers in mutual TLS scenarios receiving a client CompressedCertificate are affected. Servers that do not request client certificates are not vulnerable to client-initiated attacks. Users can mitigate this issue by setting SSL_OP_NO_RX_CERTIFICATE_COMPRESSION to disable receiving compressed certificates. The FIPS modules in 3.6, 3.5, 3.4 and 3.3 are not affected by this issue, as the TLS implementation is outside the OpenSSL FIPS module boundary. OpenSSL 3.6, 3.5, 3.4 and 3.3 are vulnerable to this issue. OpenSSL 3.0, 1.1.1 and 1.0.2 are not affected by this issue.
impacts.exploitation: Exploitation in the wild is not established by the cited description.

title: Out-of-bounds write in PKCS12_get_friendlyname UTF-8 conversion
ai_system: AISLE autonomous analyzer (specific model/version not disclosed)
summary: A crafted PKCS#12 BMPString friendly name containing a non-ASCII code point can trigger a one-byte write before an allocated buffer through the public `PKCS12_get_friendlyname()` API. The vendor says `PKCS12_parse()` takes a different path and is not affected.
ai_role: AISLE’s January 26, 2026 article says its autonomous analyzer found all 12 CVEs in OpenSSL’s January coordinated release, and individually names this case. OpenSSL’s own vulnerability record credits the named Aisle Research finder(s) for CVE-2025-69419; OpenSSL’s January 27 security advisory gives the flaw and report chronology. The exact model and division of AI versus researcher analysis are not public. OpenSSL credits Stanislav Fort (Aisle Research) as finder; AISLE says its autonomous analyzer found all 12 cases. Exact human/AI division is not published.
classification_note: OpenSSL published the vendor advisory and released fixes on January 27, 2026. The AISLE public AI attribution article appeared January 26, one day before the public vendor disclosure. No claim of in-the-wild exploitation is made.
remediation_note: OpenSSL 3.6.1, 3.5.5, 3.4.4, 3.3.6, 3.0.19 and 1.1.1ze (premium-support branch). See the OpenSSL advisory for affected release details; FIPS impact and exceptional configurations are stated in the advisory where applicable. This record does not establish deployment.

impacts.conditions:
CNA description: Issue summary: Calling PKCS12_get_friendlyname() function on a maliciously
crafted PKCS#12 file with a BMPString (UTF-16BE) friendly name containing
non-ASCII BMP code point can trigger a one byte write before the allocated
buffer.

Impact summary: The out-of-bounds write can cause a memory corruption
which can have various consequences including a Denial of Service.

The OPENSSL_uni2utf8() function performs a two-pass conversion of a PKCS#12
BMPString (UTF-16BE) to UTF-8. In the second pass, when emitting UTF-8 bytes,
the helper function bmp_to_utf8() incorrectly forwards the remaining UTF-16
source byte count as the destination buffer capacity to UTF8_putc(). For BMP
code points above U+07FF, UTF-8 requires three bytes, but the forwarded
capacity can be just two bytes. UTF8_putc() then returns -1, and this negative
value is added to the output length without validation, causing the
length to become negative. The subsequent trailing NUL byte is then written
at a negative offset, causing write outside of heap allocated buffer.

The vulnerability is reachable via the public PKCS12_get_friendlyname() API
when parsing attacker-controlled PKCS#12 files. While PKCS12_parse() uses a
different code path that avoids this issue, PKCS12_get_friendlyname() directly
invokes the vulnerable function. Exploitation requires an attacker to provide
a malicious PKCS#12 file to be parsed by the application and the attacker
can just trigger a one zero byte write before the allocated buffer.
For that reason the issue was assessed as Low severity according to our
Security Policy.

The FIPS modules in 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, 3.3 and 3.0 are not affected by this issue,
as the PKCS#12 implementation is outside the OpenSSL FIPS module boundary.

OpenSSL 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, 3.3, 3.0 and 1.1.1 are vulnerable to this issue.

OpenSSL 1.0.2 is not affected by this issue.
impacts.exploitation: Exploitation in the wild is not established by the cited description.

title: glibc tdelete could write past its stack array while rebalancing a deep tree
ai_system: AISLE AI-native analyzer (specific model/version not disclosed)
organization: AISLE, in partnership with Red Hat
summary: Calling tdelete on a sufficiently deep tree could write one pointer past an alloca-allocated stack array. The source describes a difficult trigger requiring a tree with at least about one million nodes; the written pointer is not directly attacker-controlled, and no affected application in common distributions was identified.
ai_role: The glibc security advisory credits “AISLE in partnership with Red Hat” as the reporter. AISLE’s itemized CVE page says “Discovered by AISLE.” The sources do not disclose the model/version or divide work between the analyzer and human researchers.

impacts.conditions: Calling tdelete on a sufficiently deep tree in the GNU C Library version 2.1 to 2.44 may write one pointer past the end of an alloca-allocated array on the stack, which may crash the application. The tdelete implementation keeps an explicit stack of parent nodes for rebalancing, which is grown as needed while descending the tree. Two rebalancing branches push an additional entry without checking the capacity, and write past the array when the stack is exactly full. Triggering this requires a node at a depth of exactly 40 (or 40 plus a multiple of 20), which implies a tree with at least a million nodes, so an attacker must drive a large number of insertions and deletions through an application that uses tsearch and tdelete. The written value is a pointer into a tree node and is not directly attacker controlled. No affected application in common distributions has been identified. CWE-121 Stack-based buffer overflow
impacts.exploitation: The cited source does not state whether this issue was exploited in the wild.

title: glibc EUC_JISX0213 conversion could loop without consuming input
ai_system: AISLE AI-native analyzer (specific model/version not disclosed)
organization: AISLE in partnership with Red Hat
summary: On crafted EUC_JISX0213-to-UCS-4 conversion, glibc can retain a pending second code point after an E2BIG result and emit it repeatedly without consuming input. A retrying application can hang; the path requires attacker-controlled text, a small output buffer, and use of this uncommon charset.
ai_role: The glibc advisory credits AISLE in partnership with Red Hat as reporter, and AISLE’s itemized case page says “Discovered by AISLE.” The model/version and human/model work split are not disclosed.
classification_note: The glibc advisory gives Public-Date 2026-08-26; AISLE’s specific case page was dated 2026-09-15 and provides the public discovery attribution. These dates are kept separate. No in-the-wild exploitation claim is made.
remediation_note: The glibc advisory lists fix commits for releases 2.45, 2.44-31, 2.43-56, 2.42-89 and 2.41-158. Red Hat provides mitigation guidance and distinguishes this EUC_JISX0213 defect from the related SHIFT_JISX0213 case.

impacts.conditions: Converting crafted EUC_JISX0213 input to UCS-4 or the internal wide character encoding, for example with iconv, in the GNU C Library version 2.3 to 2.44 may result in the converter making no progress, causing the calling application to hang. If the output buffer has room for only the first one, the converter stores the second in the conversion state and returns E2BIG, but it never clears that pending character after emitting it on the next call. The converter then keeps emitting the pending character without consuming further input, so an application that retries the conversion loops forever. The input must be attacker controlled and the application must convert it with an output buffer small enough to split the two code points. Only the EUC_JISX0213 character set is affected, which is not commonly used.
impacts.exploitation: The cited source does not state whether this issue was exploited in the wild.

This case requires the documented privileged kbrequest/init use of openvt -u and a TTY ownership timing condition; it is not presented as affecting standard deployments.
remediation_note: The upstream kbd commit 78d5ae1 requires both matching process ownership and controlling terminal, rejects root as a pre-authenticated target, and documents the constraint. Red Hat lists fixed errata for several product branches; do not infer that every downstream installation has deployed a fix. Until fixed, Red Hat recommends avoiding openvt -u in privileged kbrequest/init setups or disabling that binding.

impacts.conditions: The CNA description states: `openvt -u` is intended to identify the owner of the current VT and then execute `login` as that user from a privileged context. In the documented `kbrequest`/init usage, the ownership test in `authenticate_user()` relies on `stat("/proc/ /fd/0")`. `stat()` on `/proc/ /fd/0` follows the symlink to the underlying TTY device node. As a result, `buf.st_uid` reflects the owner of the TTY node rather than the owner of the process holding the file descriptor. If the TTY owner returns to `root` or the getty owner after logout while an unprivileged process still has `fd 0` attached to that TTY, the check can incorrectly treat that process as belonging to the privileged console owner. Once that check succeeds, the `-u` path executes a passwordless login as the selected user. In the documented `kbrequest`/init deployment using `openvt -us`, this can result in passwordless `login -f root` on the spawned VT. This report establishes that privilege escalation path for that documented deployment; it does not claim equivalent reachability for deployments that do not use `openvt -u` from a privileged `kbrequest`/init path.
impacts.exploitation: Exploitation in the wild is not established by the cited description.

title: libstdc++ parallel std::search could access past an undersized KMP border table
ai_system: AISLE AI-native analyzer (specific model/version not disclosed)

summary: In libstdc++ parallel mode, the Knuth-Morris-Pratt std::search implementation allocates a border table for N pattern entries but accesses index N. title: AISLE-discovered FFmpeg EVC decoder reachable assertion
ai_system: AISLE AI-native engine (specific model/version not disclosed)
summary: A crafted EVC access unit that yields no frame can still take the success path, leaving a null frame reference that triggers an assertion and aborts the decoding application.

remediation_note: FFmpeg commit 33b0107 checks the decoder return state before accessing the frame reference. Distributor release status is not generalized.

impacts.conditions: FFmpeg through 9.0.2 contains a reachable assertion vulnerability in libxevd_receive_frame() in libavcodec/libxevd.c that returns success when an access unit produces no frame. Attackers can supply a crafted EVC file with truncated or picture-less access units to trigger the av_assert0() on frame->private_ref, aborting any decoding application. Reachable Assertion
